misconceptions.statement: Air is empty space so it cannot press on anything.
misconceptions.why: Air is invisible and feels like nothing.
misconceptions.fix: Air is matter with weight, and the weight of the air above us presses on everything.

probe.question: Does the air around a table press on it?
probe.wrong_answer: No, air is nothing so it does not press.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
misconceptions.source_hint: research on children's ideas about air and gases

misconceptions.statement: Atmospheric pressure is only there when wind is blowing.
misconceptions.why: Students notice air force only in wind.
misconceptions.fix: Air presses all the time, even when still, because of its weight.

probe.question: On a calm day is there air pressure?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only when wind blows.

misconceptions.root_belief: force exists only when something visibly moves

misconceptions.statement: If air pressed on us so hard, we would feel crushed, so it must be small.
misconceptions.why: We judge size of a force by whether we feel it.
misconceptions.fix: The pressure is very large, but fluids inside our body push outward with equal pressure, so we feel nothing.

probe.question: Why do we not feel the huge air pressure on our body?
probe.wrong_answer: Because it is very small.

misconceptions.root_belief: if I do not feel it, it is small
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student ideas about air pressure

misconceptions.statement: Air presses only downward because of gravity.
misconceptions.why: Weight is always pictured as a downward pull.
misconceptions.fix: Air pressure acts in all directions, up, sideways and down, on any surface.

probe.question: A sheet of paper is held vertically. Does air press on its sides?
probe.wrong_answer: No, air only presses downward.

misconceptions.root_belief: weight effects act only downward
misconceptions.source_hint: studies on pressure in fluids and gases

misconceptions.statement: Air pressure on the upper side of a tilted glass is greater than on the lower side.
misconceptions.why: Students think more air lies above so it pushes harder on top surfaces only.
misconceptions.fix: At the same place the pressure on every side of a surface is the same.

probe.question: A card covers an inverted full glass. Why does water not fall when glass is turned sideways?
probe.wrong_answer: Air only pushes down so it cannot hold the card sideways.

misconceptions.root_belief: direction depends on where the mass lies

misconceptions.statement: Air pressure is the same at the top of a mountain as at sea level.
misconceptions.why: Students think air is everywhere in equal amounts.
misconceptions.fix: Pressure decreases with height because there is less air above, so it is lower on mountains.

probe.question: Is air pressure at a mountain top higher, lower, or same as at sea level?
probe.wrong_answer: Same.

misconceptions.root_belief: a quantity is uniform everywhere
misconceptions.source_hint: misconception studies on atmosphere and altitude

misconceptions.statement: Air pressure is greater at higher places because they are closer to the sky.
misconceptions.why: Students link nearness to the sky with more air.
misconceptions.fix: Higher up there is less air above pushing down, so pressure is smaller.

probe.question: Where is pressure greater, at a hill top or valley?
probe.wrong_answer: Hill top, closer to the sky.

misconceptions.root_belief: closer to the source means more effect

misconceptions.statement: Air pressure itself pulls things; suction is a pull by empty space.
misconceptions.why: The word suction suggests something pulling.
misconceptions.fix: Nothing pulls; higher outside pressure pushes things toward the lower-pressure region.

probe.question: What pulls the liquid when you suck with a straw?
probe.wrong_answer: The vacuum pulls the liquid up.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student explanations of suction

misconceptions.statement: When we drink with a straw, our mouth sucks the liquid up by pulling it.
misconceptions.why: The action feels like pulling with the mouth.
misconceptions.fix: Sucking lowers the pressure inside the straw, and the air pressure on the liquid surface pushes it up.

probe.question: Can you drink with a straw on a place with no air? Why?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the mouth pulls the liquid itself.

misconceptions.root_belief: the active person does the work directly
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of student ideas on drinking with a straw

misconceptions.statement: Pulling the syringe plunger drags the liquid in as the plunger attracts it.
misconceptions.why: The plunger appears to draw liquid towards itself.
misconceptions.fix: Pulling the plunger lowers pressure inside, so the outside air pressure pushes the liquid in.

probe.question: Why does liquid enter a syringe when plunger is pulled?
probe.wrong_answer: The plunger pulls it in.

misconceptions.root_belief: visible mover directly pulls the object

misconceptions.statement: A suction cup sticks because it glues or pulls the wall with suction.
misconceptions.why: It seems to stick like glue.
misconceptions.fix: Pressing out air lowers pressure under the cup, and the outside air pressure pushes the cup onto the wall.

probe.question: Why does a rubber suction cup stick to a tile?
probe.wrong_answer: It sticks to the tile like glue.

misconceptions.root_belief: sticking needs an attracting substance
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student ideas about suction cups

misconceptions.statement: A suction cup would stick even better in a vacuum.
misconceptions.why: Students think more suction means no air at all.
misconceptions.fix: A suction cup needs outside air pressure to push it, so in a vacuum it would fall off.

probe.question: Will a suction cup stick on the Moon?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, even better because there is no air.

misconceptions.root_belief: more of a cause means more effect
misconceptions.source_hint: studies on vacuum and suction concepts

misconceptions.statement: The mercury in a barometer is held up by the vacuum above it.
misconceptions.why: Students assume the empty space does the holding.
misconceptions.fix: Mercury is held up by the atmospheric pressure pushing on the mercury in the dish.

probe.question: What holds up mercury in a barometer tube?
probe.wrong_answer: The vacuum at the top holds it.

misconceptions.root_belief: empty space has an active effect

misconceptions.statement: A wider barometer tube would hold a taller mercury column.
misconceptions.why: Students think more mercury needs more force so greater height.
misconceptions.fix: Height depends on air pressure only, not on the tube width.

probe.question: A wide tube replaces a narrow one. What happens to the height?
probe.wrong_answer: It becomes taller.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

misconceptions.statement: When the barometer reading falls, air pressure has increased.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse reading direction with pressure direction.
misconceptions.fix: A falling reading means the air pressure is falling, often a sign of stormy weather.

probe.question: The mercury level drops. What happened to air pressure?
probe.wrong_answer: It increased.

misconceptions.root_belief: a measuring scale shows opposite of reality

misconceptions.statement: Water always boils at 100 degrees Celsius whatever the pressure.
misconceptions.why: Students memorise 100 degrees as fixed.
misconceptions.fix: Boiling point rises with pressure and falls with lower pressure, so water boils below 100 degrees on mountains.

probe.question: At what temperature does water boil on a high mountain?
probe.wrong_answer: 100 degrees Celsius.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from one condition works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: A pressure cooker cooks faster because it has more heat or a stronger flame.
misconceptions.why: Faster cooking is linked to more heat.
misconceptions.fix: Trapped steam raises pressure so water boils above 100 degrees, and the hotter water cooks food faster.

probe.question: Why does food cook faster in a cooker?
probe.wrong_answer: The flame is stronger inside.

misconceptions.root_belief: one visible cause explains the result

misconceptions.statement: The whistle of a cooker lets out air so pressure is the same as outside.
misconceptions.why: Students think the whistle is just a vent for noise.
misconceptions.fix: The weight over the vent lets steam escape only when pressure inside becomes too high, keeping it safe.

probe.question: What is the cooker whistle for?
probe.wrong_answer: It keeps the pressure equal to outside at all times.

misconceptions.root_belief: safety parts just make a sound

misconceptions.statement: Ears pop at altitude because the ear gets blocked by outside noise or cold.
misconceptions.why: Popping is felt along with other changes in a flight or hill drive.
misconceptions.fix: Pressure outside drops while air trapped in the middle ear stays higher, and popping is air moving to equalise.

probe.question: Why do ears pop in a fast climb up a hill?
probe.wrong_answer: Because of the cold.

misconceptions.root_belief: the most noticeable change is the cause

misconceptions.statement: Ears hurt because the air in our ear has escaped completely.
misconceptions.why: Students think pain needs a loss of air.
misconceptions.fix: The pain is from unequal pressure on two sides of the eardrum, not from absence of air.

probe.question: What causes the ear pain at altitude?
probe.wrong_answer: Air in the ear has all gone.

misconceptions.root_belief: discomfort means something is missing

misconceptions.statement: A pressure difference is not needed; a force can be applied just by air touching a surface.
misconceptions.why: Students look at a single side only.
misconceptions.fix: Net push appears when pressure on one side is greater than on the other.

probe.question: A lid has equal air pressure on both sides. Is there a net push?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the air pushes it down.

misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single cause
